lead: This unit shows how forces hold solids and liquids in shape, how materials stretch, sag, flow and grow with heat, and how that whole picture breaks down near the speed of light. After it you can compute a wire's extension, a beam's sag, a fluid's viscosity, a liquid's surface tension and a rail's expansion gap, and you can apply the time-dilation and length-contraction formulas.
about: The unit begins with Newton's laws and the three conservation laws (1.1), the bookkeeping for any system of particles or a continuous body. Chapter 1.2 turns force into stress and deformation into strain and defines the Young's, bulk and rigidity moduli. Chapter 1.3 bends a beam to measure Young's modulus and explains why girders have I-shaped sections. Chapters 1.4 and 1.5 carry the same force balance into liquids: viscosity from a sphere falling at terminal speed, surface tension from a drop breaking off a tube. Chapter 1.6 makes temperature a source of strain, with thermal stress, bimetallic strips and expansion joints. Chapter 1.7 ends where Newtonian mechanics fails, near the speed of light, with the postulates, time dilation and length contraction.

chapters.idea: Newton's three laws give every collection of bodies one rule: internal forces come in equal and opposite pairs, so only outside forces can change the total momentum, energy or angular momentum.
chapters.depth: Force, inertia, the three laws stated in words and as ΣF = dp/dt. Inertial and non-inertial frames. Action–reaction pairs and why they cancel inside a system. Conservation of linear momentum (recoil, rocket thrust), work–energy theorem and conservation of mechanical energy, angular momentum and Kepler's equal areas. Centre of mass for a rigid body and for a continuous body such as a rod. Galilean velocity addition and relative velocity (a swimmer crossing a river). Universal gravitation as the standard central force. Some syllabi open the unit with older mechanics — lever, Archimedes' principle, Copernican model, Kepler's laws — one or two lines each is enough.

figure.title: One rule for any system
figure.aria: A five-step flow: mark the system, list external forces, apply ΣF = dp/dt, set the net external force to zero, and read off constant momentum because internal pairs cancel.

chapters.example: A cricket ball of mass 0.16 kg arrives at the bat at 30 m/s and leaves in the opposite direction at 20 m/s. Contact lasts 0.010 s; take the incoming direction as positive. Initial momentum p₁ = 0.16 × 30 = 4.8 kg·m/s. Final momentum p₂ = 0.16 × (−20) = −3.2 kg·m/s. Change = −8.0 kg·m/s. Average force = −8.0 ÷ 0.010 = −800 N, that is 800 N opposite the incoming ball.
chapters.trap: Momentum is a vector: a reversal adds the speeds (30 + 20), it does not subtract them. Internal forces cancel only when the equation is written for the whole system, not for one body.
chapters.prereq: School-level Newton's laws, vectors, and the derivative as a rate of change.
chapters.leave: Rotational dynamics and moment of inertia go to the torsional pendulum in Unit 2; the first law of thermodynamics as an energy statement goes to a thermodynamics course; wave motion to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Stress spreads force over area, strain measures the fractional deformation, and their ratio is a constant of the material — but only inside the elastic limit.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach elasticity at full depth; keep it tight. Deforming and restoring force. Stress = F/A in N/m²; strain is a pure ratio with no units. Three kinds: longitudinal (tensile and compressive) with Young's modulus Y, volume with bulk modulus K, shear with rigidity modulus G (some books write η or n). Poisson's ratio σ = lateral strain ÷ longitudinal strain. Extension of a wire ΔL = FL/(AY). Stress–strain curve: proportional limit, elastic limit, yield point, ultimate strength, fracture; ductile and brittle materials; elastic hysteresis. Energy per unit volume = ½ × stress × strain, in J/m³. Steel has Y ≈ 2×10¹¹ Pa.

figure.title: Stress against strain for mild steel
figure.aria: A stress–strain plot: stress climbs in a straight line to about 400 MPa, then bends over and flattens near yield before falling as the specimen breaks.

chapters.example: A steel wire 2.0 m long and 1.0 mm in diameter hangs a load of 5.0 kg. Y = 2.0×10¹¹ Pa and g = 9.8 m/s². Radius r = 0.50 mm = 5.0×10⁻⁴ m, so A = πr² = 7.85×10⁻⁷ m². Force F = 5.0 × 9.8 = 49 N. ΔL = FL/(AY) = (49 × 2.0) ÷ (7.85×10⁻⁷ × 2.0×10¹¹) = 98 ÷ 1.57×10⁵ = 6.2×10⁻⁴ m. The wire stretches 0.62 mm. Stress = F/A = 6.2×10⁷ Pa = 62 MPa and strain = 62×10⁶ ÷ 2.0×10¹¹ = 3.1×10⁻⁴.
chapters.trap: Diameter is not radius — halving it becomes a factor of 4 in the area. Mixing moduli: a wire pulled lengthwise uses Y, a body squeezed all round uses K, a face pushed sideways uses G.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 — force, equilibrium, and action–reaction pairs inside a stretched body.
chapters.leave: Torsion of a cylinder, couple per unit twist and the torsional pendulum go to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A bent beam has one face stretched and the other compressed about a neutral surface, the resisting moment depends on the shape of the cross-section through I, and that fixes how far the beam sags.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a full chapter; keep it to the two standard cases. Neutral surface and neutral axis. Bending moment M and radius of curvature R related by M = YI/R, with Y the Young's modulus and I the second moment of area about the neutral axis. I = bd³/12 for a rectangle of breadth b and depth d, with d measured along the load; I = πr⁴/4 for a circle. Cantilever of length L with load W at the free end: δ = WL³/(3YI), which becomes δ = 4WL³/(Ybd³) for a rectangular strip. Beam on two knife edges with the load at the middle (non-uniform bending, pin and microscope method): δ = Wl³/(4Ybd³), so Y = Wl³/(4bd³δ). Some syllabi call the pure-couple case uniform bending and run it as a separate experiment. Why girders have I-sections: a thin web holds the flanges apart, so a given mass gives a large I; bridges and building frames use this.

figure.title: From load to sag
figure.aria: Four steps: a tip load creates a bending moment, the moment is balanced by YI/R, and integrating gives the free-end sag WL³/3YI.

chapters.example: A steel cantilever 0.50 m long, 20 mm wide and 5.0 mm thick carries a 0.50 kg load at its free end. Y = 2.0×10¹¹ Pa and g = 9.8 m/s². I = bd³/12 = (0.020 × (0.0050)³) ÷ 12 = 2.08×10⁻¹⁰ m⁴. W = 0.50 × 9.8 = 4.9 N. δ = WL³/(3YI) = (4.9 × 0.125) ÷ (3 × 2.0×10¹¹ × 2.08×10⁻¹⁰) = 0.6125 ÷ 124.8 = 4.9×10⁻³ m. The free end sags 4.9 mm.
chapters.trap: In I = bd³/12 the cube sits on the dimension parallel to the load, that is the strip's thickness, not its breadth. And L must be in metres like I; a length left in mm makes the answer wrong by 10⁹.
chapters.prereq: 1.2 — stress, strain and Young's modulus Y.
chapters.leave: The beam as a spring and its oscillation go to Unit 2; shear force and bending moment diagrams to a strength-of-materials course.

chapters.idea: Viscosity is friction inside a flowing fluid; a small sphere falling slowly reaches a steady terminal speed where drag plus upthrust balance its weight, and that speed gives η.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities cover the measurement in full; keep the derivation short and the numbers honest. Newton's law of viscosity F = ηA(dv/dx), with η in Pa·s and 1 poise = 0.1 Pa·s. Water ≈ 1×10⁻³ Pa·s, glycerine ≈ 0.8 Pa·s, air ≈ 1.8×10⁻⁵ Pa·s. Streamline and turbulent flow; the Reynolds number named and its meaning in one line. Stokes' law F = 6πηrv for a sphere of radius r moving at speed v, valid for slow steady laminar flow in a fluid extending far from the sphere. Terminal velocity vₜ = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η), with ρ the sphere's density, σ the fluid's. Measurement: time the ball between two marks and divide the distance by the time; wall and finite-jar corrections matter in a narrow tube.

figure.title: Speed of a steel ball in glycerine
figure.aria: A speed–time plot: the ball's speed rises steeply from zero and levels off at about 6.9 cm/s, drawn as a flat reference line, the terminal speed.

chapters.example: A steel ball of radius 2.0 mm and density 7800 kg/m³ falls in glycerine of density 1260 kg/m³ and viscosity 0.83 Pa·s. Take g = 9.8 m/s². vₜ = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/(9η) = (2 × (2.0×10⁻³)² × (7800 − 1260) × 9.8) ÷ (9 × 0.83). The top is 2 × 4.0×10⁻⁶ × 6540 × 9.8 = 0.513, the bottom is 7.47, so vₜ = 0.069 m/s = 6.9 cm/s. Between marks 20 cm apart the ball takes 0.20 ÷ 0.069 = 2.9 s.
chapters.trap: Use the density difference (ρ − σ); a ball as dense as the liquid has zero terminal speed. Radius, not diameter, and radius squared. Convert poise to Pa·s before substituting, and time the fall only after the ball has stopped accelerating.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 — force balance, plus upthrust from school physics.
chapters.leave: Bernoulli's equation, Poiseuille flow and pipe design go to fluid mechanics; the Reynolds number is only named here.

chapters.idea: Molecules at a liquid surface have fewer neighbours and extra energy, so the surface acts like a stretched membrane with tension T = F/L, and weighing a drop that breaks off a tube measures it.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach the drop weight method in detail; keep it short. Surface tension T = F/L in N/m, numerically equal to surface energy per unit area in J/m². Molecular reason: work is needed to bring a molecule to the surface. Angle of contact and the shape of the meniscus. Capillary rise h = 2T cosθ/(ρgr). Excess pressure 2T/r inside a drop and 4T/r inside a soap bubble. T falls as temperature rises; detergent lowers T. Drop weight method: a drop grows at the tip of a tube of radius r until its weight almost balances the surface tension force round the rim; the falling drop is smaller than the hanging one, so a correction factor f from tables is applied: T = mg/(2πrf). Weigh n drops and divide by n to get m.

figure.title: Drop weight method
figure.aria: A downward flow: a drop grows at the tube tip, weight pulls it down while surface tension holds the rim, and it breaks off when the two nearly balance, giving T = mg/2πrf.

chapters.example: Water drips from a tube of radius 1.0 mm. Thirty drops together weigh 1.20 g, and the correction factor for this tube is f = 0.87. Mass of one drop m = 1.20×10⁻³ ÷ 30 = 4.0×10⁻⁵ kg, so mg = 4.0×10⁻⁵ × 9.8 = 3.92×10⁻⁴ N. Without correction T = mg/(2πr) = 3.92×10⁻⁴ ÷ (2π × 1.0×10⁻³) = 0.062 N/m. With the correction T = 0.062 ÷ 0.87 = 0.072 N/m, which is water's value at room temperature.
chapters.trap: The radius is the tube's radius at the tip, not the drop's, and one drop's mass goes into the formula, not the total. The correction factor divides the uncorrected value; it does not multiply it.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 — force balance on the hanging drop.
chapters.leave: Capillarity in soil and wicks and the full derivation of excess pressure are only summarised; interference and thin films go to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A solid's length grows in proportion to its temperature change, and if that growth is blocked the same amount turns into a stress YαΔT large enough to buckle a rail.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities extend this beyond the standard three results; keep it practical. Linear expansion ΔL = LαΔT, with α per °C, the same size as per K; areal β ≈ 2α and volume γ ≈ 3α. Values: steel 12×10⁻⁶, copper 17×10⁻⁶, brass 19×10⁻⁶, aluminium 23×10⁻⁶, invar about 1×10⁻⁶ per °C. Thermal stress in a rod held at both ends: σ = YαΔT in N/m², force = σA. Bimetallic strip: two metals of different α bonded together; on heating the larger-α side becomes longer, so the strip curves with that side outside; used in thermostats, fire alarms and old clocks, and the curvature grows with ΔT and with (α₁ − α₂). Expansion joints: a gap of LαΔT in rails, bridge decks and pipelines, and roller supports under bridge girders.

figure.aria: Two bonded layers, brass on top and iron below; on heating the brass expands more and the strip curves with the brass on the outside.

chapters.example: A steel rail is 20 m long and fixed at 25 °C. α = 12×10⁻⁶ per °C, Y = 2.0×10¹¹ Pa, and the hottest day reaches 55 °C. ΔT = 55 − 25 = 30 °C. Free expansion = LαΔT = 20 × 12×10⁻⁶ × 30 = 7.2×10⁻³ m = 7.2 mm, which is the gap the expansion joint must allow. If the rail cannot move, the stress is YαΔT = 2.0×10¹¹ × 12×10⁻⁶ × 30 = 7.2×10⁷ Pa = 72 MPa.
chapters.trap: ΔT is the change, not the temperature: 25 °C to 55 °C is 30, and the same number works in kelvin because only the difference matters. A coefficient quoted per °F must be converted before use.
chapters.leave: Heat capacity, calorimetry and heat transfer go to a thermodynamics course; the bimetallic strip inside a thermometer circuit belongs to a measurement course.

chapters.idea: Because every observer measures the same speed c for light, moving clocks must run slow and moving lengths must shrink by the same factor γ.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach relativity inside this unit; keep to the postulates and the two consequences. Inertial frames and the Galilean transformation x′ = x − vt; why velocity addition fails for light. Michelson–Morley experiment: no fringe shift when the apparatus is turned, so no ether wind, and the ether idea is dropped. Two postulates: the laws of physics are the same in every inertial frame, and c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s in vacuum for every observer. Loss of simultaneity. Lorentz factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²). Time dilation Δt = γΔτ with Δτ the proper time. Length contraction L = L₀/γ, along the motion only. Velocity addition stated without algebra, Lorentz transformation written without derivation, and the spacetime interval s² = c²t² − x² as the quantity all frames agree on. One line each on p = γmv and E = γmc² with rest energy mc².

figure.title: Lorentz factor against speed
figure.aria: A plot of γ against v/c: it stays close to 1 at everyday speeds and rises steeply as v approaches c, with the muon's point marked at 5.03.

chapters.example: A muon is created 10 km above the ground and travels down at v = 0.98c. Its proper lifetime is 2.2 μs and c = 3.00×10⁸ m/s. Then v/c = 0.98, so γ = 1/√(1 − 0.9604) = 1/√0.0396 = 5.03. Lab lifetime = γ × 2.2 μs = 11.1 μs. Distance = v × time = 0.98 × 3.00×10⁸ × 11.1×10⁻⁶ = 3.3×10³ m. Without dilation it would travel only 0.98 × 3.00×10⁸ × 2.2×10⁻⁶ = 0.65 km, so the muons reach the ground.
chapters.trap: Proper time is the time on the clock present at both events — it is the shortest time, so you multiply it by γ, never divide. Length contraction acts only along the direction of motion; a moving sphere keeps its width across the motion.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 — inertial frames, relative velocity and Galilean velocity addition.
chapters.leave: The Michelson interferometer as an instrument goes to Unit 4; Maxwell's equations to Unit 3; black body radiation and the photoelectric effect to Unit 6.
